subtopic: POSTPONEMENT OF THRONE SPEECH DEBATE TO CONSIDER LEGISLATION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: POSTPONEMENT OF THRONE SPEECH DEBATE TO CONSIDER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the debate on the address will commence this afternoon, and the desire that has been apparent on the part of all hon. members to deal with those items which are of immediate importance legislatively, I have a suggestion to offer to the house for its consideration.
The supplementary estimates will be tabled today by the Minister of Finance. As you will recall, on the opening day, by leave of the house, the committees of supply and ways and means were set up in order to expedite the business of the house. The legislative program now in the form of government notices of motion covers aid to small business, housing, anti-pollution measures, the setting up of a productivity council, measures respecting vocational training and other matters. I hope the house will agree that there should be no delay in getting ahead with consideration of the legislative program right through to third reading on the resolutions in question that are already on the order paper, as well as the earliest opportunity of dealing with the supplementary estimates.
I therefore propose, and in doing so hope for the support of the opposition, that at the conclusion of the speech of the leader of the C.C.F., provided that the debate is concluded today in so far as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Argue) and myself are concerned, the debate then be adjourned by whoever gets the eye of the Speaker to a date to be determined later on, and that we return to consideration of the speech from the throne at such time as may be appropriate and in any event upon completion of the events to which I have made reference.
However, if what I hear on the radio has any basis in fact and the speech of the Leader of the Opposition is as long as has been indicated in anticipation, it may well be that my reply and the speech of the leader of the C.C.F. will not proceed until tomorrow, in which case I would hope that if the C.C.F. in its wisdom, provided the official opposition
move a vote of non-confidence, move a subamendment, the vote on the subamendment might take place before the conclusion of tomorrow's sitting and that we might then proceed on Wednesday with the legislative program.
Someone will say, what about private members' days and hours? At the same time I think it would be appropriate that these hours and days reserved to private members, and which must be maintained, should be postponed without prejudice in any way or loss of the traditional privilege which private members have and must continue to have to place the views of themselves and their constituents before the house and the country. I hope such an arrangement might be arrived at by agreement, because from the beginning it has been apparent that there is a desire to get ahead. We are ready. All we ask is that the house, in whose control we are, will agree to what I have placed before it, and that we shall be able then in an expeditious manner to deal with these matters which are of urgent moment.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: POSTPONEMENT OF THRONE SPEECH DEBATE TO CONSIDER LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all members of the house will have listened with great interest and, I hope, great satisfaction to what the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has just said. I would like to reassure him at the very beginning that I have no desire to emulate Mr. Castro of Cuba in the length of my first speech at this session of parliament. I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that after I have spoken it may even be possible to go further than the Prime Minister has indicated in reducing the time for words and increasing the time for action.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. J. Broome (Vancouver South) moved
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CANADIAN PREFERENCE IN GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-4, to provide for a Canadian preference in government construction, purchase and service contracts.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CANADIAN PREFERENCE IN GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CANADIAN PREFERENCE IN GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS
speechtext:
For many years the government's declared policy has been that there should be a Canadian preference when public money is spent on supplies. The various pronouncements outlining this policy are directive only and have no legal sanction. Further, there is no uniformity among various departments of government in applying this policy, the decision being left in many cases to the individual purchasing agent. Finally, the directives do not cover work or service contracts, and even on manufactured goods

are out of date as they do not apply to crown corporations or crown agencies such as the C.N.R.
The purpose of this bill is to declare this preference in terms as wide as possible and to give the preference legal effect, to the end that as much as possible of the public moneys so spent stimulate the Canadian economy, increase gross national production, and are returned in proportionate degree to the fund of public moneys as income and corporation taxes.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

maintopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-32, to amend the Criminal Code (nuisance).

maintopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very important bill, and at the insistence of hon. members around me I should like to explain it. In explaining the purpose of this bill, Mr. Speaker, I cannot do better than repeat the illuminating and inspiring words used by the Prime Minister when he introduced an identical bill in this house on February 28, 1955. I use the Prime Minister's words with relish.
Mr. Speaker, as provincial legislation has proven ineffective to control the wanton pollution by municipalities and industrial concerns of interprovincial rivers, the purpose of this bill is to amend the Criminal Code to provide punishment for the offence of water pollution.
This amendment is demanded by tens of thousands of people, literally hundreds of thousands in this country, who are asking for some action on the part of the federal government to protect them from the cupidity of those who, because of their power, believe they can with impunity deny the use of these waters to present and future generations.
I am glad to note the indication in the throne speech, Mr. Speaker, that the government has given serious consideration to this problem.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON MONTREAL MEETINGS
speechtext:
May I ask

subtopic: THREATENED RAIL STRIKE

My colleagues the Minister of Transport and the Postmaster General and I met with the representatives of the negotiating committee of the non-operating unions, and then we met with the presidents of the two major railways in this country. We had a very cordial

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of fhe Opposition):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I would begin, as is customary, by congratulating the mover (Mr. Maclnnis) and the seconder (Mr. Paul) of the address in reply because of the honour that was conferred on them and their constituencies by the invitation given them to take on this responsibility, and also because of the way in which they discharged it. With the straw that was available I think they were quite successful in making a respectable number of bricks.
May I also offer my congratulations to the four new members who have been introduced into this house. I know the house will understand if I perhaps underline my satisfaction at the appearance of three on this side of the house, and of those three, particularly two who are on this part of this side of the house, the hon. members for Niagara Falls and Labelle.

I should also like to congratulate the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Flemming) on his arrival in the House of Commons, something which I did my unsuccessful best to prevent. However, I wish him well during his tenure of office in this new and important portfolio. I suppose the minister's arrival is part of that process, about which we heard so much during the recess, of strengthening the cabinet which is, I know, an objective as important to the government as its necessity was obvious to everybody else. It is true, of course, that these by-elections, or two of them, were caused by the translation of members of the government into other spheres which are more exalted and perhaps even more comfortable.
This gives me an opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to pay my respects to those two members, Mr. Brooks and Mr. Pearkes. They are gentlemen who served their country over a long span of years, in war and in peace, with devotion and distinction; and in war, certainly with gallantry which, in respect of Mr. Pearkes, has become almost legendary in our military history. I am quite sure, Mr. Speaker, that in war these two gentlemen inspired fear in the opposition. In the House of Commons they inspired respect and regard in the opposition and, indeed, an affection which we were happy to share with their supporters on the other side of the house.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I hope, Mr. Speaker, the ministers who have been given new portfolios, and those who have been promoted into the cabinet, will have happiness, health and satisfaction in their new work. Perhaps I can associate with that hope for satisfaction in their work those who have been advanced from the ranks or who have been retained in their previous positions as parliamentary secretaries.
Mr. Speaker, this is a discussion of the speech from the throne, a speech from the throne for which, in our constitutional system, the government is responsible, because it gives government policy, government plans and government proposals for the parliamentary session. Therefore the government, of course, takes responsibility for the words that have been uttered in that speech by His Excellency. At least, Mr. Speaker, that is what the speech from the throne is supposed to do; it is supposed to give government plans, government policies and government legislative proposals, though we recall that last year important proposals were made by the Prime Minister in his own speech from the throne after the first one had been presented on opening day.

The Address-Mr. Pearson
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne that we are discussing at this time mentions-and this is normal, of course-a great many subjects in a very general way. During the course of this session, between now and its closing-some time, we hope, earlier than next August 15-there will be opportunity for discussion of all these subjects which are mentioned in the speech from the throne. We will have opportunity to deal with each one in turn as it appears before us in the form of a specific proposal from the government. Therefore there is no need for me to repeat now in a general way what I will be saying, or what we on this side will be saying, when these special subjects come before us for consideration. I think that course is all the more advisable at this time in view of the circumstances of economic emergency which we face.
In general our main criticism-and indeed it is a strong criticism-of this speech from the throne is that it does not reflect that situation of emergency or, indeed, the seriousness of the present situation, both in our country and indeed in the world.
Perhaps I might just say one word about the latter part of that statement, the situation in the world. Internationally, as I am sure all members of the house realize, the position is serious. It is serious enough, and the picture is sombre. At the United Nations assembly, which is still going on, the attitude and, indeed, even the antics of Mr. Khrushchev and his echoes and imitators have shown us once again, this time in graphic and indeed even in frightening fashion, the great gulf that divides democratic freedom from totalitarian tyranny, and the ever-present threat to peace and security, indeed, even to survival, that this gulf represents.
The United Nations has become a somewhat confused and worrying reflection of a new and turbulent world, with the largest group of members now, some of them without much experience in international affairs, from Asia and Africa. There seems to me no doubt that changes will have to be made in the structure of our world organization to reflect these other changes that have taken place in the world, and I am thinking in particular of the emergence of nations of Asia and Africa. I am glad, therefore, that proposals are being made for this purpose in which Canada and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) is playing an active and constructive part.

There is another subject, Mr. Speaker, that we will be discussing separately, because its vital importance requires a special discussion, when the opportunity arises. I am thinking of national defence. When the time comes to discuss national defence we on this side will seek to find out what the policy of the government is, and particularly in respect to nuclear weapons, where the position which in our minds has already been difficult to understand, has been made more confused lately by statements of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) which contradict the position previously taken and made known in this house by the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

After more than three years the proposal now made by this government to the provinces for a new deal amounts, in effect, to "do it yourself" in the three fields of taxation. speechtext: Would the Leader of the Opposition permit a question? Will the hon. gentleman say whether he is now repudiating the position previously taken by a former leader of his party, who enunciated the principle that the power which spends the money should be the power which raises the money?

speechtext:
That interruption does not make any sense and I am not going to take up the time of the house by dealing with it now, because we shall be dealing with this matter later. If the hon. member would read page 5290 of Hansard of March 25, 1907,

The Address-Mr. Pearson
the second column, he would get a complete answer to that statement. To support my own statement, I add that equalization means that in respect of the tax fields concerned the level of return in those provinces which are the least prosperous would be brought up to the level of the two highest in per capita terms by grants made from the federal government. This means that as the per capita amount goes up in the two wealthier provinces it will go up in the other provinces as well.
The proposal made to the provinces at the conference held in October does repudiate that principle by freezing equalization payments over a period of years at a fixed amount irrespective of what happens to the income in the categories I have mentioned in the wealthiest provinces. If that is not repudiation I do not know the meaning of the word. It is all perfectly clear, and all the provincial premiers know it, too, as hon. gentlemen opposite would realize if they read the comments made by them when they returned to their provinces, we have those comments on the record.
But by far the most important subject in the speech from the throne is the economic situation. We face in this country at the present time a serious situation in particular with regard to unemployment. This speech does not reflect in any adequate way the seriousness of the situation which has developed, as we said last spring it would, and which is still developing. There is an alarming complacency about this subject in this speech from the throne which is inexcusable as we face the problems and dangers before us, and as we face the effort and sacrifice which will have to be made by all Canadians in order to meet and solve these problems and remove these dangers.
For instance, the speech persists in talking of expansion in a kind of self-satisfied manner. It talks of continued expansion when, in fact, expansion in this country at the present time in respect of those factors which are so vital for development-national income and industrial employment-has ceased. The statistics show that beyond any possibility of contradiction. Even the Minister of Finance, a few months after his optimistic declaration of last spring, now admits that we have something in this country called a rolling readjustment, which means recession.
There is no awareness in this speech of the seriousness of the unemployment situation, no feeling of any kind that there is an emergency. In this regard the speech is shocking in its lack of awareness. Why, the word "unemployment"-the very word-is not even mentioned in the speech, although there are a lot of words in it. Perhaps that is not
strictly accurate. It is mentioned once as part of the title of an act, the Unemployment Insurance Act, I think. That is the only occasion on which even the word is used. Why, even last year, in January, it was mentioned once alongside the word "seasonal". Yet no person can deny or ignore or gloss over the fact that in October of this year 117,000 more persons are out of work, or 42 per cent more than at the same time last year; that unemployment figures in October-368,000-are higher than in any October since pre-war days on the basis of a calculation which we now all of us, I think, accept in this house; we do not need to argue about figures any longer. Perhaps that is some progress.
No one can deny that 5.7 per cent of the labour force is out of work as against 4 per cent a year ago, against 5.3 per cent in October, 1958 when we were facing a difficult time in the employment field, 3.4 per cent in October of 1957. That was the situation, 3.4 per cent which the government inherited in terms of unemployment. Moreover, the percentage is, of course, going up at a rate which if not checked-and it will not be checked by the proposals in the present speech from the throne-will result in a figure exceeding the 10 per cent high of last winter. That is a grim picture as we face the months ahead, yet this speech talks, not about unemployment but continued expansion.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I wish there was evidence of continued expansion which would justify that applause. Let us see what the evidence is to support the statement I have just made. The volume of our national production per capita is now lower than it was in 1956. There are many other signs showing that we are now suffering from lack of growth momentum resulting in stagnation. During the second quarter of 1960 the gross national product, which is an important index, of course, actually declined by 1.5 per cent-

It declined by 1.5 per cent
over the period in the previous year. That is the first decline since the final quarter of 1957 and the biggest drop since the quarterly data became available. There are other indications showing that we are going through what the Minister of Finance now admits to be a period of recession or "rolling readjustment". Indeed, according to experts whom I have consulted-and the hon. gentleman knows them, too-that situation began in March, 1960.

The Address-Mr. Pearson
The unhappy fact-and it is an unhappy fact-is that the predictions concerning such a situation which we made in this house during the last session when we were jeered at as being prophets of doom and gloom; the predictions which we made in this house at that time, and the minister can look them up, are being shown as too conservative, too cautious.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: So you are happy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I heard that silly jeer, "You are happy". It is a measure of the seriousness which the hon. member attaches to this problem. We shall get a lot of this kind of interruption during this debate. Every time we call attention to facts bearing on the seriousness of the situation in order to make the government aware of it so that it can take some action, we shall be jeered at as being satisfied and gloating and happy about it. An interruption of that kind is not worthy of any hon. member in this house.
Perhaps such an interruption might have been justified if we had made predictions last session, and the session before, which had, in the event, proved false. The fact is that the falsification has taken place in the optimistic predictions, in the statements by spokesmen for the government that everything was all right. Their optimistic predictions-and if I had time I could quote page after page of them from Haiisard-are now shown to be both unrealistic and unjustified.
What does the government intend to do about it, at least in terms of this speech and in terms of immediate action for creating employment? The speech includes certain proposals which may or may not be good in themselves-we will have a chance to examine them-but certain proposals which will be of no help for this emergency in terms of jobs this winter. All the government proposals in this field referred to in the speech involve either grants or loans to individuals, to private business, to municipalities or to the provinces, so that the impact of these proposals on employment will depend primarily on the initiative and the financial capacity of individuals or public authorities other than the federal government.
The speech also includes some proposals which were already publicized before parliament met. Indeed, some which were announced in the last session appear again in this speech. The speech also includes some proposals or what could be described as watered down versions of proposals which we on this side have been advocating for some time, and which were rejected by the government on previous occasions. That is the package, gaudily wrapped up.

I do not want to take very much time, especially in view of the Prime Minister's remarks at the beginning of this sitting, but if I had time I could put on the record the proposals which we on this side of the house made last session dealing with this serious unemployment situation. Those members of the house who were here will recall that my colleagues and I did just that on more than one occasion. I recall a statement made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) following a speech I made in which some of these proposals were put forward. His statement may be found at page 1698 of Hansard of March 3. Referring to my remarks the hon. gentleman said:
I appreciate his-
-that is, my-
-realistic approach to this problem and the suggestions he has made are good and those suggestions are good for action to be taken in the future.
I regret that the government has not decided to take action along the lines I suggested at that time, in spite of the minister's reaction. For instance, there is nothing in the speech-in the government's package, as it were-for export industries, although I know that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) is calling all the trade commissioners back to Ottawa; nor is there anything for secondary manufacturing industries or for agriculture, at least for the immediate future. Neither is there anything for the Atlantic provinces, though there are some proposals for development in other parts of Canada.
In this connection it might be well to recall that we on this side have already advocated a capital assistance fund or what might be described as a capital grants fund for the Atlantic provinces. That, indeed, was in our program of 1958. Perhaps the scope of a fund should be extended beyond the Atlantic provinces to cover any area of Canada where economic development was lagging behind the national average. We propose that such a capital assistance fund for national development should be established by parliament and administered according to certain fixed principles, and not on a hit-or-miss basis for political advantage. We will have something more to say about that when we get down to consideration of the detailed proposals of legislation.
To return to the speech from the throne itself, we will as outlined in general terms in that speech, not be in a position to deal with the government program, to assess it satisfactorily, to support it when it is adequate and to expose its inadequacy, until the individual items are before us in terms

of definite proposals for action by this parliament at this time. Moreover, we will not be able to see what these proposals mean or do not mean, especially in terms of the employment emergency which we now face, until the supplementary budget is brought down, this appears to us to be an essential part of the government program. It is very difficult to assess the significance of some of these more general items in the speech from the throne until that supplementary budget has been presented and examined.
That should be done at the earliest possible date. And as it is a budget, and not the kind of financial statement we got in 1957, there will be opportunity for a full review by the Minister of Finance of the economic state of the nation when he presents it and opportunity for a full analysis of that review by us on this side. This is an absolutely essential part of any government program at this time which is designed to deal with unemployment in this country, and I am glad that the Minister of Finance obtained permission to introduce a supplementary budget at this juncture.
As far as this immediate and urgent problem of unemployment is concerned, our examination of it must include not only the proposals in the speech from the throne when they are brought down in terms of definite and concrete legislation, but it must include the supplementary estimates which were tabled today. Although I have been able to only cursorily examine those supplementary estimates, they do not seem to me to be very impressive in terms of creating work. Our examination must also include a detailed scrutiny of the supplementary budget to which I referred.
In my view our examination of these things should begin at once so that action can be taken immediately where action is required. Surely this is not the time for a general debate extending over eight days. Indeed, we were debating these matters in this house from January last until the middle of August. If the government and its majority insist on further debate at this time, or at some time after a temporary interruption they can, of course, arrange that that course be followed; but if they do so they will be responsible for further delay in taking the action necessary to provide jobs. That is our first responsibility in this house at this time.
I repeat, surely it would be better for us to have the discussions and debates which must, of course, take place on specific questions before us, on the supplementary budget, on the supplementary estimates, on the legislative proposals for action embodied as they are in the speech from the throne, and
The Address-Mr. Pearson on those specific plans which the Prime Minister on September 21 said he had ready in detail for presentation to this session of parliament. Let us then receive and discuss these specific proposals with a minimum of delay. If the specific measures introduced by the government to deal with unemployment or other economic problems are good ones, we on this side will support them. If they need to be improved, we will recommend improvements. Surely, Mr. Speaker, this is the right procedure to follow in this serious situation which we face. It is certainly the right procedure for a responsible opposition to produce and to follow.
At this time the need is for specific action instead of general talk and, for that purpose, for consideration at once of budgetary proposals and other legislative measures. So, to facilitate this possibility of quick action on concrete matters I do not intend now to move an amendment to the address which would, of course, be bound to start a general debate. Instead, we on this side propose to follow the course adopted by the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett at the opening of the session of 1930 when parliament faced a very serious unemployment situation and serious unemployment problems. At that time the leader of the opposition, Mr. King, did not move an amendment and at that time Mr. Woodsworth also did not move an amendment. The prime minister, Mr. Bennett, proposed that the debate on unemployment measures should begin at once and that was done.
Similarly, in 1935 when Mr. Bennett was prime minister, on the eve of an election and at a time when unemployment was still a very serious problem in the country, the leader of the opposition, Mr. King, did not move an amendment to the address and Mr. Woodsworth, the leader of the new party at that time, which was then called the C.C.F. party, also refrained from moving an amendment. However the government at that time did not seem to have its legislative proposals in order and there was a delay of a few days before there could be a discussion of them.
That is the course that we propose to follow at this time, Mr. Speaker, the course adopted in 1930 and 1935 when this parliament faced serious and emergent employment problems.

speechtext: May I ask the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) a question on that point? In 1935 Mr. King, the then leader of the opposition, spoke for over three hours without moving an amendment. Does the Leader of the Opposition intend to do the same thing today?

speechtext: That will be something new.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I should add at once that no such amendment on our part is needed to show our lack of confidence in the present government, a lack of confidence which we know, from gathering evidence on every side, is shared by a great and growing number of Canadians.
So, Mr. Speaker, the course I have proposed, if it is followed, will make possible the adoption this evening of the motion thanking His Excellency for his speech immediately after the leader of the C.C.F. party has spoken, assuming, of course, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) does not take up the remainder of the time this afternoon and this evening. If that can be done and we can take the vote early this evening -it is now only four o'clock-then we can begin at once consideration of the urgent business before us, the supplementary estimates, the supplementary budget and the other legislative proposals, four of which are now on the order paper in the form of resolutions.
We can tackle at once, without a further seven days of general discussion, our most urgent domestic problem, unemployment. It is true we will have less time for talk if we adopt this course but we will have more time for action.
The situation which we face in our country today, Mr. Speaker, the slowing down of our expansion, the "rolling readjustment" of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), the mounting unemployment, surely this demands this departure from our normal procedure because these are not normal times. Canadians look to this parliament for leadership and for action, so let us give the Canadian people that action from the very beginning of this session by, in these urgent circumstances, abandoning the seven days of general discussion and beginning the discussion of legislative proposals at once.

I felt a sense of appreciation for the attitude taken by the opposition in accepting immediately the setting up of these committees as being tantamount to an attitude in confirmation of confidence in the government.
It is a very interesting commentary on parliamentary life, that the fiery effusions of the last three months on the part of the Leader of the Opposition when he was outside the house became pusillanimous and uncertain in the delivery of his opening speech today. There was a tremendous change. I am not going to read what he said about what was going to happen, the manner in which we were going to be devastated and the frightening challenges that were going to be made. I waited for these challenges. I prepared. The preparation was unnecessary.

Then, when he found out-

speechtext:
Then, when he found out we were going to call a session, he demanded it. He has taken a sinuous course during the last few months. He demands after he realizes that action will be taken.
I looked forward to his suggestions today, suggestions that would have been beneficial but which so far he has kept concealed. We

want to know what suggestions the opposition has. We heard about them during the course of recent events across the country. We thought they might be amplified in the House of Commons. I say at once that we accept what we, indeed, asked for, not only by requesting the setting up of the committees on Thursday last but through the statement I made at the opening of the session today when I placed before the opposition the opportunity to do that which, above everything else, we want to do; namely bring into effect at the earliest possible date the comprehensive proposals that we have placed before parliament.
I do not intend to traverse the field as I expected I should have to do. The very fact that the Leader of the Opposition has restricted himself makes it necessary that I do the same, and that I do not go into the particulars with regard to the legislative program but rather proceed with the resolutions at the earliest possible time that are today on the order paper; and, having secured the passage not only of the resolutions but of the bills based thereon, that we then proceed with an examination of the supplementary estimates, to the end that parliament will act early and efficiently. It was for this reason that the house was convened in the fall.
I found out during the years, and against my earlier judgment, that parliament, to be efficient, required changes in the rules. Indeed, at the last session in my opening speech, I suggested the setting up of the rules committee. It was constituted; it operated and it brought forth recommendations that will be beneficial, that will make for a more efficient House of Commons. However, before I deal with the only problem selected by the Leader of the Opposition, that of the economy, I must follow the usual course by extending my thanks and joining with the Leader of the Opposition in offering congratulations to the mover (Mr. Maclnnis) and seconder (Mr. Paul) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The hon. member for Cape Breton South, a man from the labour ranks, speaks with the authority of labour in this House of Commons. The hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere gave an indication in his address of the degree to which he is making himself, and has made himself, eloquently bilingual. Both these hon. members made a contribution to parliament and both discharged their responsibilities in a manner in keeping with the traditions of parliament.
I join with the Leader of the Opposition in welcoming the new members, and I particularly welcome the new lady member of the house. She will join the other lady members here. One of the peculiarities of our political 90205-6-4
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker system has been the fact that during the years few women have been elected to the House of Commons. I cannot, at the moment, say what the number has been but it has been comparatively few. If we could think of all of them, it would not take long to repeat their names and their contributions. We welcome the other hon. members. We know something of their standing in their respective communities. Each has a contribution to make and I can say to them, on the basis of my experience of more than 20 years, that each of them will find in the House of Commons an atmosphere in which differences of opinion, frankly and clearly expressed, do not diminish mutual respect.
I should like to say a particular word on behalf of the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Flemming) who, in the field of provincial politics and administration, has given great leadership in New Brunswick. I now expect him in the House of Commons, in the larger field in which he is particularly qualified, to carry out those responsibilities which will rest upon him, within, of course, the constitutional limitations imposed upon that department.
Many of the cynics say it is an impossibility for private members to make a contribution in parliament. This is not what I have found. They have influence and I need only point to one item as indicative of the contribution private members can make. There is a sentence in the speech from the throne which states simply that you will be asked to consider a means of encouraging the youth of Canada in amateur athletics. This is indicative of what has been done by three hon. members-and I am not placing them in order of their importance in the contributions made-the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Weichel), a distinguished veteran of the first world war and a well known sportsman; the hon. member for Hamilton South (Mr. McDonald), a great rugby player whose career in sports was cut short by an affliction which would have stopped a less courageous person; and the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor) who, in his own right and as the son of Cyclone Taylor, has done so much in the armed forces and since on behalf of sport in this land. These three members pressed on parliament, and through parliament to the people, the need for something to be done in this regard. This government accepted the suggestion for we believe in doing those things which will make a great Canada. In the field of sports today there are tremendous dividends in national pride from some degree of success in athletics. The uncommitted countries of the world are now using these athletic contests as measurements of the evidence of the

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker strength and power of the nations participating. I am not going to say anything further with regard to the contributions these hon. members made.
Now, sir, I wish also to extend my congratulations to the newly appointed leader of the C.C.F. He is in a rather unique position, and I say so with the kindest of good feeling for him because what he leads is about to die. Since the days of Mr. Coldwell it is the first occasion on which a person has received an honour such as this while a member of the House of Commons. All I can say to the hon. gentleman is this. While the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Pitman) allowed himself to be taken in by the C.C.F. for introduction purposes, he is not going to carry that procedure beyond the introduction.
I now intend to pass from that field which is traditional in the House of Commons and which must be dealt with in keeping with tradition. I am going to say a word on the economic side. The Leader of the Opposition, that adjectival authority, spoke in sonorous tones, not gloating but glooming. He pictured the darkness spreading over Canada, something he has been doing over and over again. He spoke of the seriousness of unemployment. There are none who do not recognize this problem as a serious one not only in Canada but in the United States. Strangely enough, at this time these two nations are forging ahead; they are expanding and developing. Yet while expansion takes place they are both having a degree of unemployment which none of us can regard with complacency. This government has not regarded this problem with complacency.
The hon. member today made a statement which at least was the first admission in that regard, namely that we inherited an unemployment rate of 3.4 per cent. There have been increases since we came into office; there were decreases as well. But we in Canada have followed much the same course as in the United States-although the increase in our unemployment has been somewhat slower. I have here the figures to which I will make reference in a moment. These indicate a trend in both our countries that challenges all of us, without regard to our position, to do what we can in order to bring about an increase in the field of employment.
I said that our Canadian economy is moving forward. His Excellency the Governor General in his address refers to that fact. There was no admission on the part of the Leader of the Opposition to that effect; the whole picture was one of gloom. There was on his part no attitude of making suggestions that might meet a situation that faces us all.
I need not point out that the previous government between 1936 and 1940 had a higher percentage of unemployment than that which exists today or has existed at any time since the war. I think this is something that must be told to the Canadian people for, after all, the opposition would lead them to believe that they now have a solution to this problem.
I said that the Canadian economy is moving forward. New record levels will be achieved in many important sectors. Total employment during the year was the highest in Canada's history and labour income the highest. Consumer spending and commodity exports have been increasing to a degree that few people could have believed possible even a year ago. In the first half of the year the gross national product increased by 3 per cent to $35.34 billion at seasonally adjusted annual rate. This figure was lower than that we had hoped for. The economists in Canada and in the United States had expected otherwise.
One year ago at this time it was the general view of economists that we in both our countries had passed the point when unemployment might increase. All the reports were that the recession was terminated or was coming to an end. In the third quarter of the year a number of important economic indicators have firmed and increases in the national product over the second quarter are indicated. In any event, for this year as a whole, the result will be another record year in gross national product.
We are not satisfied; we are not complacent. That is the reason for the legislative program that we brought before parliament in 1957, 1958 and 1959. That is the reason why at this session of parliament we intend, by the legislative program not only to expand the effort of the federal government but with the assistance of provincial governments which have a responsibility in this matter and of the municipalities, business and labour to endeavour to bring about by united action an end of this problem in our country, or a diminution of the difficulties in this regard that face this country.
The hon. gentleman spoke about an economic emergency. There is no economic emergency in Canada. There are difficulties. Those who try to leave the impression on this country and on its people that we are indeed in chaos economically, and in the general growth of our country, are doing a disservice to Canada and to the Canadian people. Were it not for the fact that I intend to restrict my remarks I could quote the previous prime minister of Canada, Mr. St. Laurent, fortified by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin).

As to the progress made by Canadian industry in 1960, is the picture that which the Leader of the Opposition endeavours to place before parliament?

There has been an increase in the volume of production of many important items such as steel ingots, newsprint, sawn lumber, copper, nickel, lead and Canadian produced motor vehicles. The Leader of the Opposition gives you a picture of fear. For what purpose? Why speak of an economic emergency when everything points to the contrary? There was none of that sort of thing in the United States election. In so far as unemployment is concerned their record is such that their percentage, figured on the index we use in Canada, would be much higher than it is in Canada.
What do they say? Both leaders have said that, excepting in certain areas-coal mining areas, and in the automobile production areas -these things have come about as a result of automation, technological advances and those things over which there is no immediate control. These are the figures-and they speak of darkness and gloom. They sow, in the hearts of Canadians, fear that everything is wrong.
These are some of the figures. Steel ingot is up 3.3 per cent from January to October; newsprint is up 6.6 per cent between January and September; and from January to August sawn lumber is up 7 per cent; copper is up 14 per cent in the same period; nickel is up 21.2 per cent; lead is up 5.6 per cent; zinc is up 1.3 per cent; motor vehicles shipments are up 1.7 per cent from the January to August period. I repeat that there is a higher labour income than ever before, and more people are employed in Canada than ever before.
Then what about personal expenditures on goods and services? They amounted to some $11 billion in the first half of 1960, 4 per cent above the level for the same period in 1959. Retail sales were higher during the first nine months of 1960, but not as high as we would hope, being but one half of one per cent higher.
Ruin-that is the slogan. That is the banner that the opposition has put up-and fear. Is it any wonder that we keep referring to the fact that that famed expectant leader of the Liberal party, that radio man from Toronto, said "Our one hope of getting back into power is depression"? I hope and trust that his views have not become the anchor of the party as a whole.
One of the most encouraging developments in 1960 has been the achieving of a record level of commodity exports; and even more noteworthy is the fact that this was ac-90205-6-ii
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker complished despite the levelling off in sales to the United States, which is Canada's most important market. Total commodity exports for the first nine months of 1960 amounted to just under $4 billion, 8 per cent more than the same period of 1959.
Then they talk of economic chaos and of emergency. This gain was made possible by significant increases in sales to overseas countries. Canada's exports to the United States were only about one tenth of one per cent above the 1959 level. There are those who write from Canada to British newspapers and picture the darkness of the economic situation of this country as though trade between the United Kingdom and Canada was being reduced. These are the figures. Shipments to the United Kingdom were 20 per cent higher in the first nine months of 1960 than in 1959. Our exports reached the peacetime record of $676 million. Sales to other commonwealth countries were up by 21 per cent, and exports to countries other than commonwealth members and the United States were 23J per cent higher than during the first three quarters of 1959.
I called together representatives of business and industry on October 24. There was none of this fearsome attitude on the part of Canadian businessmen. They recognized the problem that had been brought about through failure to act in 1956, and then amplified and increased by the advances in technology since 1950.
I could go on from there and give you the overseas countries which purchased substantially more in Canada in this period. Australia, Japan, France and west Germany are among the important countries showing major gains in purchases from Canada during the first nine months of 1960, compared with the same period in 1959. For 1960 as a whole, prospects are for a gain of 6 to 8 per cent over the record 1959 export total of 5.1 billion dollars. Where did these markets come from? From preaching fear?
As soon as we assumed office we sent a group to the United Kingdom for the purpose of encouraging trade. The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Churchill)-the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as he then was- went over with them, and the results have been phenomenal, and beneficial not only to Canada but to the United Kingdom.
Do you know why there was no quotation today on the part of the Leader of the Opposition in support of his message of gloom and doom? It was because he realized that these facts existed and it would be better not to deal with statistics, except in a general way, by lumping everything together and calling it, in the most caustic of tones, economic uncertainty and chaos in the land.

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker
What about our commodity trade? The increase achieved in commodity exports and the maintaining of the 1959 level of imports has reduced the adverse balance of trade for Canada, for nine months, from about $415 million in 1959 to $121 million. There is something that has to be faced. Throughout the years, the adverse balance of trade has been anything but beneficial to Canada. You remember in 1956 the general adverse balance for the United States was some billion dollars. What do they say now, those who belonged to the government of that day who were selling out to the United States? They were selling out Canada's birthright for depreciated United States dollars. That is the interpretation of the words of the Leader of the Opposition.
What about the years from 1950 to 1957 and the adverse balance of trade during that period? It would appear that for political purposes they would undersell Canada. That is something that I do not believe is representative of the thinking people of Canada.
What were the adverse balances of trade from 1956-and this is commodity trade? In 1956 the figure was $713.2 million. That is why we say they were selling out Canada. In 1957 the figure was $589.2 million; in 1958, $156.1 million; in 1959, $368.6 million. From January to September, 1959, the figure was $414.7 million; from January to September, 1960, $120.5 million.

If the hon. gentleman would allow me to carry on I should be obliged to him.
I point out that we have maintained our exports and that the result I have brought to the attention of hon. members has arisen because imports have not increased in the same percentage as exports and this at a time when the opposition goes across Canada saying "Aren't things terrible?" There was reason for the Leader of the Opposition not to follow his usual course of quoting statistics on this occasion.
What about prices in general? Price levels have remained fairly steady through 1960. There has been an increase in the cost of living index mainly, I am told, in connection with food. The consumer price index is slightly ahead of 1959 during the first ten months of the year. The wholesale price index has been stable throughout 1960. At mid-October last the index stood at 230.3, slightly higher than its October, 1959 level of 230.
A moment ago I mentioned the labour force. The labour force has grown rapidly

over the years from 6,290,000 in October, 1959 to 6,499,000, or by about 3J per cent which compares favourably with the annual rate of increase in the labour force between 1946 and 1959 which was 2 per cent. The economy has been able to absorb a very substantial part of this increase. While employment in each month of 1960 so far has continued to be at the highest level for that month in history, there are still many who are unable to secure jobs. It is to these that our concern must naturally be directed.
In the first ten months of the year employment averaged 5.95 millions which is
102.000	more than for the same 10 months of 1959, the previous record level. I am not going to take the time of the house to discuss the reasons for the current abnormal increase in the number of Canadians seeking to enter the labour force, but that is one of the underlying factors coupled with continuing mechanization. Our economy is in a period of transition from post world war II and Korean war conditions to one which we hope means peace. There are difficulties and there are adjustments. When I hear hon. gentlemen opposite saying that they have a solution for the problem I simply take these figures between 1936 and 1940 and base them on the new relationship between labour and unemployment which came into effect in September, and we find that-and I am taking this period because in those years the figures were not covered throughout the year-by which time the government of that day had been in office some seven or eight months, it was 13.5 per cent. In 1937 it was 9.6 per cent; in 1938 it was 12 per cent; in 1939 it was 12 per cent; and on June 1, 1940 it was 9.7 per cent. I do not refer to these statistics for any other purpose than this [DOT]-not as one of excuses or as any basis for complacency but simply so that the record may bear witness to the facts.

I mention this simply for the purpose of indicating that this problem of seasonal unemployment, accelerated and increased as a result of technology, has become more and more apparent following the end of the honeymoon period after the war when Canada and countries like Canada had a sellers' market all over the world. These statistics that I place before you are simply designed to assure that the record shall be clear. The challenge of continuing unemployment in a steadily expanding economy is one with which the government has to deal, and ever since we assumed office we have taken steps to which I shall not refer at the moment. We have continued to take steps. We have launched a national development policy. We have expanded development in every part of Canada.
We now find that further action must be taken in the interests of national development with a view to assuring that Canada shall not be priced out of the markets of the world, for without national development and trade there can be no jobs. This is what we place before this house. I can assure the house that if there are any other reasonable suggestions that emanate from any part of the house that appear to be beneficial they will receive every consideration.
We have launched a winter works program and accelerated it. We have provided a larger program of assistance to municipalities in this regard. The provinces have responsibilities, too. Last year the provinces contributed from nothing to 25 per cent of the labour costs in municipal works under the winter works program. So far this year one province, the province of Quebec, has increased its contribution to 40 per cent because of the realization quite frankly admitted by the government of that province that the responsibility for jobs is not one that rests on the federal government-

-of itself, but rests on the provincial governments and rests as well on business and labour.
There are no paying jobs at a time when men are on strike. I hope that on the one hand business will deny itself increasing profits that are unfair and unjust. Of course, profits are needed for without profits in business there cannot be jobs. On the other hand I hope that the labour leaders of this country will give heed to the national situation and do their part to assure that reason will characterize their relations with business across Canada to the end that jobs may be maintained.
I cannot resist referring to an incident that occurred in my home province. A few years ago-I think about 1945 or 1946-we had a government in Saskatchewan that said all you had to do was socialize business, establish it under the government and there would be jobs. That was all right as far as liquor was concerned and also as far as power was concerned but it did not work in the other fields. No, we must do our part to maintain Canada at this time at a level that will assure that our export trade shall not diminish for if we do not, we shall not have jobs. An amazing job was done by the present Minister of Veterans Affairs while he served as minister of trade and commerce in maintaining and developing trade. The new Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) has caught the imagination of the Canadian people with his project to bring together the trade officials of the department from all parts of the world. He can enthuse them and give them a picture of what is needed. We in Canada will have to keep our prices down, otherwise enthusiasm for export will not give rise to increases in exports.
I mentioned what we are going to do. Our program as outlined in the speech from the throne has been described as a package. I think I have heard that expression before.
I believe I heard it on the night the speech from the throne was delivered. I think the

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker word used by the speaker on the television program was "package" but I could not quite make it out. In any event, the Leader of the Opposition has seen fit to say that what we propose to do is only a package. Are winter works a package? Is the carrying out by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) of an expanding development in public works merely a package? Approval of these programs has been recommended with a desire of putting Canadians to work. That is why I am very pleased that we are going to proceed at once with the supplementary estimates and these other items of legislation.
The Minister of Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith), with a view to assuring that hospital construction should not be diminished because of the uncertainty as to whether the policy would continue beyond March, 1963, has given notice that he will recommend that these grants will be continued so that those requiring hospitals will be able to proceed with them.
Recommendations have been made concerning changes in the National Housing Act. A few weeks ago the university foundation met with me and among the recommendations they advanced was one concerning the need for loans for the construction of student residences. That is what they asked for. The Leader of the Opposition somewhat ridiculed the fact that loans were part of this plan. That is what they asked for in an effort to meet a need which exists across this country. The information I have is that this particular item has received universal support among the universities.
Let us consider the action taken in the larger field of national development. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge) read with relish some words about pollution. This is one of the most challenging problems facing Canada. By 1990, unless something is done, Canada is going to run out of wholesome water. The provinces say it is impossible to act on their own and the municipalities say they cannot. The wholesome water with which Canada has been endowed beyond the endowment of any other nation in proportion to its land area must be preserved now and to that end we are going to make available long term loans for approved projects for sewage disposal and treatment representing up to two thirds of the cost of these projects.
The Leader of the Opposition said that these undertakings will not provide action now. In order to secure action immediately a grant will be authorized to write off one-quarter of the amount of any such loans, in other words one sixth of the total amount spent on such work done before April 1963.

It will take a while for the plans to be developed. Already the city of Ottawa has tremendous plans in this regard to do something to bring about the preservation of the waters of the mighty Ottawa, one of the great rivers that played such an important role in the history of mankind's march west and that has increasingly become a floating polluted body.
Hon. gentlemen opposite say there is nothing in the government program, that it is only a package. Small business does not say it is a package. Small business across Canada has made it very clear how welcome is the guarantee for bank loans to small business to finance additions and improvements for their equipment and premises. This is something they have sought over the years, an opportunity to improve the appearance and increase the efficiency of their establishments so that they will be able to maintain that which this government believes in, fair competition for all business in Canada. This is one of the most advanced moves that has been taken by any government to bring about the assurance that the small shall have an opportunity of competition with the great.

If I may digress at this point, the Leader of the Opposition mentioned the antics of Mr. Khrushchev. From sneers and smiles to shoes, that was his attitude at the United Nations.
