The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker
week that magazine, representing the accumulation of the speeches of the week by the leaders of that country, underlines the necessity, as the Leader of the Opposition said, of realizing the gravity of the situation today and of preparing our people at the same time by the necessary training so that we will be able to meet the ever-increasing competition from the communist world.
Then there is the productivity council. I am not going to go into particulars in that regard because the measure will be before the house very shortly. It is an endeavour to bring together representatives of business, agriculture and labour, women's representatives and representatives of all sectors of the community to the end that in a community of effort, as has been successful in the United Kingdom and elsewhere, we shall secure the counsel, advice and, above all, the concerted action of these groups brought together by the state but controlled by private enterprise and not directed by the state in any way.
Then there is the larger field of public works, not to meet the needs of the moment especially but rather to meet Canada's future needs, to meet the kind of destiny that we believe Canada will have. We hope that the Columbia river agreement will be in the form of a treaty before this session is over.
There is also the opening up of the north. There were those who said we were simply building from nowhere to nowhere. Tremendous developments have taken place in highway construction. As a result of our policies 4,000 miles of road are under way, making available to the Canadian people the opportunity to develop our resources.
With respect to northern Alberta, the promise was made as far back as 1926, I think, that a railroad would be built into the north. As one of our promises in the election of 1957 we undertook to initiate the building of the Pine Point railway. When we were in a position to proceed there was a great division of opinion with respect to whether the road should proceed east or west, and that is one case where the east will never meet the west. Each side had its views. We set up a royal commission and, when an agreement has been arrived at with the two railroads, we hope to be able to proceed with this new railroad. In the meantime a detailed survey will be made so that the work can be gone ahead with on the western route.
Finally, there is a proposal that affects the city of Winnipeg. Ever since the 1800's the Red river has overflown from time to time. My own great grandparents were driven out in 1815 as a result of the floods of that day, and this situation has continued ever
since. We expect to bring before this session appropriations covering the construction of a floodway. We also intend to do something that western Ontario has been seeking for years and years. We intend to do something to conserve and control the waters of the upper Thames river in southwestern Ontario.
There is the program so far as work and development are concerned. I am not going into the other particulars at this time. However, I should like to refer to the assurance that Canada shall remain Canadian. We shall bring before the house measures to ensure greater participation by Canadians in the ownership and control of our industries and resources. That does not mean that we are opposed to foreign capital. We welcome United States capital or capital from any part of the world. In the formative days of the United States, when developments were taking place and the country was being opened up, that country demanded that investments should be not in the form of ownership of equity stock in the main but rather in the form of loans and the like.
We believe that the time has come to put a stop to the trend that we found when we came into office and which has been increasing from 1950 onward, a trend whereby the great resources of our country are being owned more and more by another country. We are not intending to discourage foreign capital and such capital will continue to come into our country because Canada affords the safest security in the world. However, we are asking that Canadians be given an opportunity to have ownership in the industries and resources of Canada and we hope that the policies of foreign companies and foreign unions will be in the interests of Canada. That is our objective.
It is a policy of Canadianism, not a narrow nationalism but rather the imbuing of Canadians as a whole with a pride in their country and the provision of the opportunity for them, and for those that follow them in all parts of this country, to have a reasonable equality of opportunity in opening up the country and making possible developments that will create jobs.
I mentioned the opening of the railroad in northern Alberta. At the same time, in the province of Quebec, the Mattagami railroad will be proceeded with. Whatever the problems, we believe in partnership in Canada. That is the purpose, the aim and dedication of this government.
Then I conclude where I commenced. Do not let us sound paeans of recession. Let us catch something of the greatness of this country. When we indulge ourselves and preach recession, it has this effect on the hearts of Canadians: It breeds depression. I am asking
46	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Argue Canadians to come out of the valleys of doubt. I am asking this house to leave these valleys. Let us mount to the hilltops of determination and faith. I say to the Leader of the Opposition that his desire to come to grips with these problems is one that will receive support from all members in all parts of the house. I want to see Canadians giving a new emphasis to Canada's greatness, to its potentialities or possibilities. Let us turn from gloom to productivity, to unity instead of class consciousness and division. That is what I hope, Mr. Speaker, will be achieved in this session; a spirit of determination to meet the problems that are facing the nation.
None of us can but have compassion and sympathy for those who are without work. But, sir, let us not multiply the numbers that are. Let us not accentuate the statistics that are factual and correct. Let us simply, at this session, proceed with this program, which is not a package but a contribution, with parliament giving the lead to new vistas of development, new expansions in international trade.
None of us can do it alone. Governments cannot do it. It will require the co-operation, as I said a while ago, of all Canadians, and I am asking the powerful, who are in business or in the ranks of labour organizations, to use their power and influence to meet these problems and thereby bring about in Canada a new expansion, new developments. I hope that this will be achieved. To that end, this government asks the support of all hon. members in all parts of the house.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words in this debate on behalf of this group are to congratulate the mover (Mr. Maclnnis) and seconder (Mr. Paul) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and to say that I believe each of them has done an excellent job in presenting the case for the government to this house and to the country. I want to associate myself with the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) in expressing our friendship for those who have been elevated to the other place in recent times, for those who have been elevated by means of a rearrangement of work within the cabinet and for those who were elevated to the cabinet for the first time and our welcome to the new members.
It is clear from the attitude of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), the attitude of the Leader of the Opposition and of this group, that members from all sides of the house are anxious that we deal expeditiously with the business that has been placed before parliament. Certainly we in this group hope that the legislation presented to the house
[Mr. Diefenbaker.)

will be adequate to deal with the major economic problems that face this country.
It is difficult for the Leader of the Opposition to know just how to approach a debate such as this. I certainly recognize that difficulty. It is difficult not only because the government says in the speech from the throne there are a number of things it wishes to do, and because the official opposition, along with us, wish to do everything we can to expedite beneficial legislation, but it is made even more difficult by the rather strange attitude taken by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister in replying to the Leader of the Opposition at first berated the Leader of the Opposition for not having moved an amendment. His theme was, if you do not move an amendment you are pussyfooting; you are expressing confidence in the government; you are pusillanimous; you have gone back and forth across this country pointing out the great difficulties that face the nation and when you have a chance to move an amendment, you fail to do so.
But the Prime Minister did not proceed long with his speech before he changed his tactics and reverted to the very opposite position. He said that the Leader of the Opposition and those around him who criticize the government are doing a disservice to Canada. In one breath he says it is all wrong not to criticize and in the next breath he says it is wrong to criticize. My position is that if there is something to be exposed and criticized, it is our job to do it and no statement by the Prime Minister accusing us of being purveyors of doom and gloom will prevent us from pointing out the failings and shortcomings of this government, of which there are many.
The Prime Minister has embarked on an extremely interesting theme. His theme is that there is no economic emergency. Those are his words. I wrote them down as he uttered them. He said, "There is no economic emergency". In view of the statistics produced by various departments; the recent actions of the people of Canada when they have had a chance to express their will in a free, democratic way; and the resolutions that have been passed by leading Canadian organizations I suggest to the Prime Minister that the evidence is overwhelming that there is an economic emergency. If there is no economic emergency in the Prime Minister's mind this may explain why the government has allowed this crisis to deepen and to worsen before it has made even a gesture of meeting these great difficulties.
The speech from the throne has in it many things but if one were not a resident of this country and did not realize the difficult economic problems we face, from a reading of it one would gather nothing to show that the

government is aware of an emergency of any kind existing at this time. When it has come to talk about unemployment the government has talked about employment. When it has come to talk about our trade imbalance, the government has talked about larger exports. When it has come to talk about recession and unemployment, the government quotes statistics to show that certain isolated segments of the economy are showing a small advance.
The unemployed in Canada will not agree with the Prime Minister when he says that there is no economic emergency. There may not be an economic emergency for those who sit around the Prime Minister but there is an economic emergency for Canadians who are out of work, and it is a serious one.
The latest statistics show that on October 15 there were 368,000 unemployed in Canada as compared to 251,000 in October of the previous year, an increase of more than 40 per cent in that period of time. I have in my hand the labour force publication of September, 1960 and September is the last month that is shown in this particular publication. If one starts with the unemployment rate in September, 1956, the year prior to this government taking office, one finds that the total of those unemployed in Canada was 116,000. One year later, September, 1957 the unemployment figure had reached 214,000 or almost twice the number. In September of 1958 the unemployment figure has reached 285,000; in September, 1959 it was down to 225,000; in September of this year it had gone up to 337,000.
I suggest that these figures destroy the statement of the Prime Minister that there is no economic emergency. The fact is that we are in a recession. We have widespread unemployment. Nothing that the Prime Minister is able to say will remove that economic fact at this time. Those who are unemployed, on reading the Prime Minister's statement, will be flabbergasted to learn that the he is aware of no economic emergency.
There is other evidence of an economic emergency. It is referred to in the speech from the throne in a rather loose and offhanded manner. It has to do with impending amendments to the unemployment insurance fund. The unemployment insurance fund in the first full month of office of this government, namely July, 1957, stood at just over $862 million. That sum has been reduced from $862 million to $319,476,000 by September of this year and the forecast is that by spring, unless action is taken, the fund may go to the low figure of $100 million.
The reason for this disappearance of the great unemployment insurance fund is the fact that Canada faces an economic crisis and an unemployment crisis and this fund has
The Address-Mr. Argue been used under the administration of this government in a way in which it was never intended to be used. This fund has been a substitute for full employment instead of a policy to take care of the income of people that are transferring from one job to another. The government, when it introduced amendments to this legislation on a former occasion, increased the benefits by 10 per cent and increased the contributions by 30 per cent. By its use of the unemployment insurance fund the government has endeavoured to load the main burden of unemployment on working Canadians and on their contributions to the unemployment insurance fund rather than take forthright action of its own in order to bring about a full employment policy.
This political party which forms the government appealed to the country in 1957 and again in 1958 on a full employment policy. It did not ask for the confidence of the people of Canada by saying there would be a third of a million unemployed or a half million unemployed or that they would be satisfied if 4 per cent, 5 per cent or 6 per cent of the working force were unemployed. This government went to the people of this country on a definite program to end unemployment, to substitute jobs for idleness. In this commitment the government has wholly failed. But the failure is not recognized by hon. gentlemen opposite. Instead, the statement is made that there is no economic emergency.
Another substantial plank in the program of this government was to end our trade deficits, to end United States domination of large sections of Canadian industry and to bring about a better balance in Canada's trade relationships. In his statement there was almost no mention by the Prime Minister today of this great trade crisis that faces Canada and of the growing domination of our country by outside capital. The Prime Minister, has not pointed out that although his policy, he states, is that Canada will remain Canadian, in his three years of administration more and more of the natural wealth and the industrial potential of this country has been alienated to citizens from other countries.
The Prime Minister feels that Canada will remain Canadian, while all the time more and more Canadian industry is falling under United States domination and control, so much so that the governor of the Bank of Canada has pointed out the great dangers to our economic life, to our national existence, from this growing control of Canadian industry from outside. He points out, also, that this growing ownership has increased from some $4 billion in 1949 to some $17 billion at the end of 1960; and he points out that the net transfer of Canada's natural wealth to
48	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Argue outside owners this year will reach the alltime high of $1J billion. That was another substantial plank in the program of this government which was a good point of salesmanship but about which the government has done nothing.
The Prime Minister has said that if there are to be jobs in eastern Canada, there must be money in the pockets of our farmers. That is a correct statement. But from what the government has been doing you would not think the Prime Minister meant what he said this afternoon. Certainly he is not following this course as a matter of government policy. He said, when he was appealing to the Canadian electorate, that one of the things that his government would do would be to provide support prices for agricultural products based on parity. His slogan for agriculture was, "We want parity, not charity". While the government has been in office there has been no charity that I know and there has certainly been no parity.
From this side of the house, the Prime Minister used to attack the former minister of agriculture for rock-bottom floor prices on agricultural products. How he castigated him for forgetting the agricultural industry of this country. Under the former minister of agriculture, and under this government, prices for basic agricultural commodities were allowed to fall below the very low floor prices of the previous administration.
Of course, this government talked one way in those days and acted in another way when it took office. The government said, in going to the country in 1958, that it would provide a system of stable prices that would give the farmer his fair share of the national income. They provided a price; not a floor price but a national average, and as long as there were not more farmers being paid less than the national average than there were getting more than the national average, then those producers who were getting less could recover nothing. The official statistics of the Department of Agriculture, economics division, show that in January, February and March of this year, even after the deficiency payment of eight cents per dozen has been taken into account the producers of Canada received less than the floor prices provided in years gone by under legislation which this government had condemned so roundly.
The experience with hogs is not over for this year. One cannot say what the final result will be; but I suggest there is evidence from the figures that can already be obtained that some producers, having received less than the national average, will have no opportunity to recover the difference between the price they have been paid and the national average.


The government talked about parity instead of charity, and instead of bringing about a strengthening of agricultural prices through legislative action, prices of agricultural products were allowed to go even lower. The Prime Minister this afternoon talked about increased trade and expanded markets. We need them. We need increased markets for agricultural products, for many products of Canada's forest manufacturing industry. Our fishermen need new markets. But there is little evidence that the government has seen its own vision, when it spoke of expanding markets for agricultural products.
When this government took office initially it began to do a number of things. In 1958, for example, it increased the home building in Canada to something over 160,000. Now, after having been in office for three years, that number will be tens of thousands fewer. Initially, this government seemed to take its commitments rather seriously in the field of increasing our export trade for wheat. In the first year of the government's administration it increased our exports of wheat by 320 million bushels. Then there was a pause, and the next year it allowed the exports of wheat to fall to 294 million bushels. Last year it allowed the exports of Canadian wheat to fall to 277 million bushels. In spite of the fact that people who know the agricultural industry say that because of low rainfall crops have been less than they are in normal times, our surplus has once again built up.
The former minister of trade and commerce was able to export 320 million bushels of wheat in his first year of office. We have a new man in charge of the marketing of Canadian wheat, and his vision is to export this year, if possible, 300 million bushels of wheat. Instead of the government taking action to move this surplus of grain on to the world markets, the vision has dimmed; the government's sight has become short. They say, "We can never attain the goal that was ours in our first year in office." When the government took office initially it provided the Colombo plan countries and other countries with 32 million bushels of wheat as gifts. After they had done this for one year they reduced the amount to 18 million bushels. For the crop year just ended the amount has been reduced to seven million bushels. The vision is fading away; the noncommercial market is disappearing.
This government says it is in favour of the commonwealth; it is in favour of action to support the commonwealth and to improve commonwealth relations. Yet this government sat idly by and forced the government of India, when it was in need of wheat, to go to the government of the United States and make a four-year agreement covering the
sale of 586 million bushels of wheat. This government has lost the opportunity of a lifetime.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Was that a sale, or a gift?

Here was a non-commercial sale; here was a chance for the Canadian government, I suggest, to share in the kind of agreement that was signed between the government of the United States and the government of India. This government turned India down, turned the commonwealth down, and has turned our prairie farmers down and condemned them to keep their grain on their farms, unsaleable, while the United States farmer increases his sale of grain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That just is not true.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question on the clarification of the words used. The hon. member spoke about a noncommercial sale to India. Was it not an outright gift?

No, it was not an outright gift, although the minister should know better than to ask a question like that. Half of it was a loan, and half of it was a gift. But that does not make it quite an outright gift.
What a non-commercial sale.

I was sorry to see the wheat board transferred to the Department of Agriculture; I think the Department of Trade and Commerce, that has to do with trade, is the place to handle the surplus commodity that should be exported. It should not come under the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) whose department is concerned with production and agricultural practices. The Minister of Agriculture has already given us evidence that his vision is dimmed. He has said: "We shall try to sell 300 million bushels of wheat" and he tells the farmers they must put some of their land into alternative use.
This government does not apparently realize that the sales of wheat in the world have not been falling but increasing. In 1952-53, 639 million bushels of wheat were sold by the four exporting countries of the world. By 1959-60 this quantity had increased to 996 million bushels, an increase of 56 per cent. In 1952-53 Canada sold 45 per cent of the market; last year we sold 28 per cent of the market. The United States in 1952-53 sold 33 per cent of the market; last year the United States sold 52 per cent of the market. The United States is forecasting that in the present crop year it will sell 570 million bushels of wheat while Canada will be relegated to a very inferior second position with a target of 300 million bushels.
The Address-Mr. Argue
This government says there is no economic emergency. Ask the grain producers who are today trying to exist on a unit quota at 925 marketing points. I want to ask the Minister of Agriculture to comment on this point. Why did he say he intended to issue weekly statements from now on? No wonder he wants to issue weekly statements. He knows he cannot withstand questioning and criticism on this score in the House of Commons, and he is trying to relegate discussion to the post office and the mailing facilities. We do not need further information as to quotas given in this way. We are circulated already every week with this information and the minister does not have to circulate alibis. He has to tell parliament and the country what the government is doing about this very serious economic crisis.
Before the last two elections the government had a vision of a united Canada. It had a vision of better federal-provincial fiscal relations, yet at the recent federal-provincial conference this government made an announcement which, if it is put into law, will turn the economic clock back at least 25 years and put Canada back into the economic tax jungle of the thirties. Canadians-and this is the fundamental thought behind equalization-no matter whether they live on the prairies, in British Columbia, in central Canada or in the Atlantic provinces should have the right to a basic equality in provincial services, and the day of equalization will, in my opinion, be gone because this government is saying: To him that hath shall be given and from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath. By fixing an amount of $220 million for the provinces over a period of five years this government has shown that it is prepared to throw the equalization provision out of the window.
The government may deny that there is an economic emergency, but I suggest that there is a political emergency in Canada, and it is in the Conservative party which today, in my judgment, no longer commands the confidence of the people of this country. The government's record is dismal and inept. Its proposals, if one can read between the lines, are inept and I suggest that the government should undertake a number of things; not a small measure of public works but a greatly extended building of public works across Canada; not just aid to municipalities but aid to provincial governments to embark on public works.
I suggest the government should raise its housing sights at least to the level of 1958. I suggest that the federal government should establish a capital investment fund to be used for investment in Canadian industry to

The Address-Mr. Argue prime the employment pump and to see if more of our industry cannot be built on the basis of Canadian ownership and control. I suggest there is need now for a great drive for markets around the world; that the Canadian government instead of opposing the development of free trade areas had better start thinking in terms of living with these free trade areas and of joining in a broad Atlantic free trade area as the only salvation for Canada's economy.
I feel it is the job of an opposition party to facilitate in any reasonable way the handling of government legislation, but I also feel it is the duty of an opposition party to challenge the government, and therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge):
That the following paragraph be added to the address:
This house regrets that your Excellency's advisers have failed to implement their election promises through refusal to undertake the economic and social planning necessary to provide full employment, a stable and prosperous agricultural community. and an adequate social security system.
I believe that having moved a want of confidence motion in reply to the motion we are discussing I now have unlimited time. However, I do not intend to take advantage of that and if I can be given a few more moments I shall conclude my remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question before he does so? When he was speaking about the wheat sales proposals of the United States he suggested they were going to sell some 500 million bushels. Would the hon. member not like to tell the house that 70 per cent of that would be a gift program?
The minister can quibble over terms if he likes-
Oh.

The fact is that the United States will sell, in the language of the wheat board, either in the commercial market or in the non-commercial market 570 million bushels of wheat at a time when this government admits failure. I suggest that instead of running into debt to foreign investors to the colossal amount of $14 billion a year some consideration should be given as to whether or not this export surplus might be used to alleviate part of this huge amount by which we are going into arrears to investors from outside.
Remember, the government knew the answers to these questions before it was given the responsibility of government. Now the government asks members of the opposition to show them the way. This was a government which was going to sell our surpluses. Instead
[Mr. Argued

of selling them it has allowed them to build up and go unsold in very large quantities.
Would the hon. member permit another question? Would be not agree that there is a relationship between strikes on the part of grain handlers and low wheat quotas?

I have been saying to the government for a long time, long before the strike came about, that it was time the ministers concerned showed some initiative in an attempt to avoid the strikes so that the workers would not lose pay and so that markets for agricultural products should not be lost.
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. member a question. By the suggestion he has made is the hon. member recommending compulsory arbitration?
Don't be silly.

"Don't be silly" is a good answer to that question. I suggest that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) should have got off his fanny many weeks ago and gone out to Vancouver, as also should his colleague the Minister of Agriculture, to try to do something about averting the strike so that the workers might be maintained in employment and the markets for wheat continued. This government may not recognize an economic crisis-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS ENTERPRISES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first may I thank the house for its co-operation which has enabled the government to proceed today with this measure.
The committee will recall that the speech from the throne contains the following paragraph:
You will also be asked to give early consideration to a bill authorizing government guarantees for bank loans to small businesses to finance additions and improvements to their business premises and equipment. My ministers are convinced that additional medium term credit facilities for small businesses would enable many private projects to go forward this winter all across Canada, providing substantial additional employment. Moreover, this addition to our credit legislation will constitute a continuing stimulus to the growth of Canadian private enterprise.
The bill to be founded upon the present resolution deals with the provision of intermediate term credit to small business. Its purpose is to assist small business enterprises in financing a wide range of capital improvements. This is a further step in the government's program to take appropriate measures for ensuring that the small businessman shall continue to share fully in Canada's economic progress.
As hon. members will recall, in 1958 a small business section was established within the Department of Trade and Commerce. This organization provides a liaison between government and small business and is charged with the responsibility for studying the problems of small business and advising as to the measures necessary to meet them. The bill to follow the present resolution follows upon such earlier action and reflects the government's intention to provide assistance to small businesses where required and in a manner which is constructive as well as beneficial for the economy as a whole.
The proposed bill provides authority for the government to guarantee bank loans to small business enterprises. The loan scheme, as it is envisaged, will take advantage of the existing network of branch banks and we can expect that the government guarantee will encourage lending and will increase the availability of medium term credit to small business. The general nature of the legislation is similar to the Farm Improvement Loans
Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses Act which has been in operation throughout the post-war period and continues to be of considerable value in the improvement and mechanization of Canadian farms.
I may say that when the bill is introduced I think all hon. members will be struck by the similarity of its form to that of the Farm Improvement Loans Act, a similarity which marks not only the scheme of lending under the provisions of the bill but many of the provisions of the legislation itself.
It is anticipated that the new measure, when placed on the statute books, will provide the same opportunities to small businessmen and will be instrumental in furthering the efficiency and competitive strength of small business enterprise. The extension of credit facilities as proposed under this measure will be of benefit to many firms and businesses across Canada and should play an important role this winter, of course, but also in the years to come in stimulating employment and economic activity generally.
I am sure I do not need to speak at length on the subject of the need for such a measure. As the government has been told in the course of representations received from time to time from representatives of small business organizations, there is a need of intermediate credit. Bank credit, of course, is available on a short term basis to business enterprises but for small businesses there is no available intermediate term credit. That is the situation that has given rise to this measure. The permissible term of loans that would qualify for government guarantee under this measure is ten years, the same as the provision in the Farm Improvement Loans Act. It is designed to provide credit for the renovation and extension of premises as well as the acquisition of equipment.
In relation to the general desire to promote measures that will be effective in creating employment during the coming winter I may tell the committee that it has been represented to us by small business organizations that the amount of contract work available in the course of renovation and extension of the premises of small retail businesses in Canada amounts to approximately $75 million. It is confidently expected that this measure will put many small businesses in a position to undertake renovations and extensions of that nature.
Questions will naturally arise as to where the line is drawn with respect to small businesses. This measure is designed to be of benefit to those who qualify under the definition of small business. To large business, of course, credit is available through security issues. That avenue of credit is not open to the proprietors of small businesses. The measure will provide a definition of what is a

Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses small business. The basis of determination of the definition that has been chosen is the gross revenue. The measure will therefore define a small business enterprise as a business enterprise the estimated gross revenue of which as stated in the application for a business improvement loan did not for the fiscal period of the business enterprise in which the application is made exceed $250,000.
The classes of business which will qualify will also be of interest to the committee, I am sure. The definition has been written in terms broad enough to include four classes of business, namely manufacturing, wholesale trade, retail trade and service businesses.
I wish to make it clear that these definitions will include the proprietors of tourist establishments. We have received from organizations representing proprietors of tourist enterprises representations in which they have indicated that while they qualify for bank loans for short periods, nevertheless they could undertake, and desire to do so, additions to their premises, but credit is not available for a long enough term. In most cases the term that has been required, in the representations that have been made to my knowledge, has been in the range of seven to eight years. This measure will provide guarantees for bank loans for terms up to ten years.
The bill lays down the conditions which the banks must meet in order that their loans to small business can qualify for government guarantee.
To recapitulate and to summarize, may I say that the purposes for which guaranteed bank loans may be made include the purchase and improvement of equipment and the extension and renovation of business premises. Loans of this kind will be available to proprietors of enterprises who carry on in the four classes of business of which I have made reference. The limit of $250,000 on the gross revenue for the year in which application is made has been established having in mind a reasonable and equitable definition of a small business enterprise. Having regard to the statistics available, I may say that it is indicated that a high proportion of all establishments of the four categories I have mentioned will qualify within the terms of the legislation as small business.
The maximum amount which may be borrowed by a small businessman-that is to say, the proprietor of a small business enterprise-is to be set at $25,000. In general, the terms and conditions of lending will be flexible and will conform, as far as is practically possible, to the individual circumstances of the borrower, taking into account the size and purpose of the loan.

In order to encourage bank lending under this program each bank will be guaranteed against loss up to 10 per cent of the aggregate of loans made by it. There will be a maximum limit on the total amount of loans made by all banks to which the government guarantee will apply, and this has been set at $300 million for the first three years of operations. In that respect the terms of the measure correspond precisely with those of the Farm Improvement Loans Act. At the end of the period that I have mentioned, namely three years of operation, parliament will be in a position to appraise the operations under the act in the light of actual experience.
We have been encouraged by the reception accorded to this measure to believe that it will be effective for the purpose for which it is being introduced. I think hon. members are aware that in the newspapers of last Friday Mr. J. P. R. Wadsworth, the acting president of the Canadian Bankers' Association, was quoted as saying he was quite sure that the banks will co-operate. Mr. A. C. Ash-forth, president of the Toronto-Dominion bank, was quoted as having said that the government proposal to enable chartered banks to make medium term loans to small business is a commendable one. Then the article attributes to Mr. Ashforth the following statement in quotation marks:
I think the government is hitting at a place that might be effective in relieving unemployment. Most banks now have sufficient money available to make loans in this field. There has been some easing ini the money supply, and I think we can take it for granted that if there is a demand for more money to make the program effective, it will be made available.
Provision of medium-term loans to small business should enable them to undertake new programs for improving their facilities and installing new equipment. This should have an effect on employment in cities and towns across Canada.
I think it is quite clear, therefore, from the statement made by the president of the Toronto-Dominion bank, that the banks have credit available and will be encouraged to put it at the disposal of small business in proper cases, in accordance with the terms of the proposed legislation.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think it may be said of this measure that it will assist small business enterprises in Canada and in that way will make a contribution to strengthening the economy and strengthening private enterprise within the economy, particularly the flowering of private enterprise in the small businessman. So far as the immediate situation is concerned, I think it is clear, that this bill, when its provisions become available, will contribute very substantially to the creation of employment in the immediate period.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS ENTERPRISES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to indicate my support and that of my colleagues for this resolution. We Liberals find it easy to support this resolution because it embodies a proposal put forward by our leader as long ago as February, 1958. To document that statement, I should like to quote from page 22 of the Pearson plan, which our leader put forward when the 1958 election was called. Under a paragraph heading of "Special provisions for small business", I quote the following:
Besides benefiting from the general improvements in business conditions noted above, small business would get special assistance from the Liberal government.
This would not take the form of free advice, or instructions on how to run a business. We believe that the individual businessman in Canada knows how to run his business and needs no interference from governments.
What we propose is tax relief for businesses earning less than $10,000 a year, by cutting the corporation tax rate to 10 per cent on profits up to $10,000 a year. Beyond that point, business would continue to pay 20 per cent (including the 2 per cent old age security tax), as all businesses up to $25,000 do now. This tax cut would save businessmen $25 millions a year.
The facilities of the industrial development bank should be extended to include retail trade. Our small merchants have faced increasing competition from the large chains and at the same time have found1 it increasingly difficult to obtain capital for improvements and expansion. It is essential that our small merchants should have the opportunity to raise capital on reasonable terms.
It is therefore with great satisfaction that we see the government adopting, even at this late date, that part of our leader's plan. This resolution-as the minister has just pointed out-is an expansion of the principle already embodied in legislation governing farm loan boards, fisheries loan boards and other bodies, such as C.M.H.C. We welcome now its extension to include small business because I think it can be argued without any doubt that the small businessman and small business enterprises are really the backbone of our Canadian economy.
The minister has told us that the definition of small business envisaged in the legislation which he proposes to bring down is one whose gross revenue is not more than $250,000 per year. I do not know what percentage of our businesses will fall within that definition. Usually not less than about 80 per cent of business enterprises come within the category of small business. That is particularly true in legislation which has been passed in the United States for a similar purpose.
Most of our provincial economies are such that small enterprises are more suitable than large ones. Economic stability depends upon orderly growth, and the well-being of small
Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses enterprises and the kind of financial assistance envisaged in this resolution is an excellent means of ensuring economic democracy and at the same time helping to overcome the unemployment problem.
In times of tight money small business enterprises are the very first victims. Large corporations can fall back on the floating of bonds and many other alternative courses of financing which are not available to the little fellow. Yet orderly financing and an orderly program of planning and improvement is just as important and just as essential to small business enterprises as to large corporations. But an orderly program of planning and improvement cannot be carried out without orderly financing.
Nevertheless many small businessmen are reluctant to take advantage of loans from a bank, even when such a loan may be available. The main reason for this, of course, is that bank loans are usually made on demand, and many small business operators feel they cannot take the risk because a sudden demand for repayment by the bank would put them out of business altogether.
The fact that this resolution will permit them to secure loans for a period of ten years will go a long way toward solving that problem. Also, when a loan is on demand, profits are tied up for four or five years in an effort to retire the loan as quickly as possible, and that leaves no opportunity for planning. These conditions are particularly hard on widows and families whose living depends upon the income from businesses of this nature.
At this stage we are merely discussing the principle of the resolution. We are in favour of the principle, but exactly how much benefit the small businessman will receive will depend upon the nature of the legislation to be introduced. It will depend upon the scope of the legislation; upon the types of loans; upon the types of businesses to be covered; the terms of the loan, and the definitions. The minister has already given us some information about this. I think it will be a source of disappointment to many Canadians that only four categories of business will be included in this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS ENTERPRISES
speechtext: These four categories take in practically everything. May I point out that they include retail, wholesale, manufacturing and service industries? #That is just about as broad as you can make it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS ENTERPRISES
speechtext:
I would like to see the cooperatives included in those categories as well as the others which the minister has mentioned. I think the co-operatives are peculiarly suited to our economy in the Atlantic provinces and in my opinion they are just as deserving of assistance of this kind from

Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses the government as the other categories which the minister has mentioned. In view of the urgency of the economic problems which face this country, and in line with the example already set today by our leader and the Prime Minister, I do not intend to say any more at this time. However, I do have a few questions which I shall ask at a later stage to elicit further information on the points I have already raised.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS ENTERPRISES
speechtext:
We in this group are certainly happy to see this resolution before us and we are especially happy to see it before us at this very early date in the current session of parliament.
I should like, merely for the record, to express also our disappointment at what has been done in the years which have already gone by. I well remember the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958 and how the Prime Minister's heart bled for the small businessmen of our nation. Then, at long last, we saw the establishment by a vote at estimate time of a branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce. The initial vote which at that time was voted to the branch which was to be organized to help small business was the sum of $30,000, hardly enough to mail a mimeographed letter to each of the small businessmen in my constituency to advise them how to make ends meet by getting more hours of work out of their wives and daughters engaged in helping them in their small businesses.
We were amazed to note that only one year later neither the sum of $30,000 nor a much larger one, as we had hoped, appeared in the blue book. There was absolutely nothing in the blue book of this year voted for this particular branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce. That is why we are especially pleased at this action which is being taken at what I like to think of as being an emergency meeting of the House of Commons; that is why we are pleased that a resolution has been placed before us with at least as much magnitude to it as the words would indicate.
In our minds our society has not yet reached the stage where we can do without ma's corner store. In our economic world and our community life she has a very valuable ^ole to play, because ma of the corner store is the first one to respond to the needs of the community as a community. We know with regret that so very often the larger business organizations have no heart; they have no soul for the needs of the immediate community. We feel that our society has not yet developed to the stage where we can abolish ma of the corner store without a severe loss in more ways than one.


I should also like to warn hon. members that if we allow real free enterprise and real competition to be abolished in the retail world the consumers of Canada are not going to get the benefit of the abolition of such competition. They are going to suffer the consequences.
Perhaps I may point out that the first and only member in this House of Commons ever to advocate a measure such as is now being proposed in the resolution before us, namely loans for the capital needs of small business, was a member of our group, the hon. member for Vancouver East. I recall the utter disgust expressed by Conservatives and Liberals in this house at that time. We had to appeal to our philosopher, the hon. member for Kootenay West, to explain adequately to the house why it was only natural that a member of our group should be honestly concerned with the survival of the individual as an individual in our society. He reminded this house that our very movement had its foundations back in 1933 because of our concern with what the forces of finance and world events were doing to the potentialities of the individual as an individual.
I regret the insufficiency of the resolution now before us although I welcome it as far as it goes. I regret its insufficiency because I am afraid it may lead to a bill, welcome as it would be, wherein the assessment might be based only on the letter of the law and I am afraid that adequate leeway will not be given to a consideration of all the important factors over and beyond the mere statistics.
I hope that an adequate number of years will be allowed for repayment. I hope, also, each individual business will be assessed on its own merits with regard to the number of years allowed for repayment. I regret the inadequacy of the resolution particularly in one major aspect. It is all very well to offer to lend someone some money, but I feel it is much more important that we should ensure the ability of the borrower to repay the money he has borrowed.
I often feel an apprehension that when the House of Commons increases loans to farmers, fishermen and people who want to own houses we do not adequately consider the ability of the borrower to honestly and honourably meet the commitments that we ask him to undertake. Sometimes I have the feeling that we are perhaps being unkind rather than kind when we offer a loan to an individual without satisfying ourselves that he will be able to meet the repayment of the loan and discharge his obligation honourably and well. In this respect I regret the lack of assurance that small business is going to be able to command buying power equal to that of the large corporations.

I have noticed price lists issued by wholesale houses concerning goods available to the retail field. They list categories a, b, c, d, and e, and the spread between categories a and e is much larger than the spread between the retailer's purchase price and his resale price. If the government really wanted to help the small businessman they ought to restore to him a measure of equity in this regard. This, more than anything I can think of, would enable him to establish a level of earnings adequate to meet his commitments and to meet the repayments that are going to be arranged for him under the terms of the bill which will follow the resolution now before us. Unless you enable the small businessman to make a satisfactory return, it is a disservice to offer to lend him money or to make loans available to him.
I regret that the intention of the government with respect to helping the small businessman has not yet been made clear. I feel that nothing would help the small businessman survive more than the institution of a graduated corporation income tax. I feel that many of the evils existing in the business world today would be eliminated through the institution of such a system. If we can defend a graduated system of income tax in respect of the income of individuals we should also be able to defend a system of this nature as applied to the income of organizations and corporations.
In the past the Minister of Finance has attempted to define his conception of what is a small business. We feel it is not as easy to define as the minister indicates. A small business may be worth $1 million in its assets or many millions in the volume of its turnover and yet, on the other hand a business with assets of $30,000 may be a large business. It all depends on what kind of business it is about which you are speaking.
A number of years ago before a meeting of the banking and commerce committee an operator of hotels in the city of Toronto appeared and testified that he owned three hotels, including one of the largest in that city, and admitted that he had to pay up to 24 per cent interest for the money he needed for the modernization of his hotels. The only sources of funds available to him were the finance companies who at that time imposed an interest rate of 24 per cent.
You might have the operator of a barber shop, for instance, where $20,000 a year would make him a big operator. You might also have the operator of a mill in the forests of British Columbia where $1 million would be a relatively small operation. I feel it is premature to impose an arbitrary limit on the amount available. Every business ought to
Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses be gauged by its nature, rather than subject to any arbitrary figure we might decide upon here.
I was pleased to note the minister's announcement that the government intended that these loans apply to the purchase of equipment as well as to the expansion or purchase of new premises. We feel keenly that if a line is going to be drawn as between large and small business, it ought to be drawn on the basis of degree of personal ownership assuming personal responsibility in management and not on the dollar volume that happens to be involved, the volume of business or the investment concerned.
I am pleased to endorse the proposition advanced by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo that co-operatives be included.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS ENTERPRISES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I tell the hon. member that co-operatives are included. They are eligible under the Farm Improvement Loans Act and they are eligible under this bill, too.

speechtext:
I am pleased that when the minister mentions manufacturing, wholesale and retail and even services, he is not too much concerned whether they are owned by individuals or by a group of individuals. If that is the case we shall have no more to say about that.
I also hope that the legislation now before us will be of assistance to the many thousands of operators of service stations who are now nothing but underpaid slaves of the major oil companies of Canada. I hope that adequate resources will be made available to them so that they will no longer be the lessees of the major oil companies and that the legislation to follow this resolution will enable these people to attain real independence so they will no longer be dictated to by the major oil companies as they are now.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I take pleasure in rising to offer a few remarks in relation to this resolution. I only wish I had the ability to unravel the line of thought of the previous speaker. I fail to see where he started or finished. The hon. gentleman talked around and about, and I do not think he arrived anywhere.

speechtext: I will be here after the next election, don't you worry.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS ENTERPRISES
speechtext: That is pretty cocky talk; a rather heady statement.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS ENTERPRISES
speechtext:
I should like to congratulate the Minister of Finance for bringing forward the important resolution that is before the committee tonight. I think this legislation to help the small businessman is one of the best

Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses pieces of legislation that has ever been introduced. Since 1957 the government has demonstrated that it is looking after the small businessman. The government looked after the workman by helping him finance his home. It looked after the farmers by increasing the amount of loan that a farmer could obtain from a bank to rehabilitate his buildings and equipment. One of the greatest needs among the farmers was for capital to moderize their old equipment and bring it up to date so they could compete. Now the small businessman will be able to get the capital he needs. Heretofore he could not get a loan for any great length of time through the banks. Now by this legislation he will be able to get a loan for ten years.
Think how important this is going to be to the tourist operators who do not have access to the normal channels of borrowing money from our lending institutions. They will now be able to rebuild and modernize their plant and equipment so that they can carry on the tourist business in a successful way. We all know how important it is to Canada today to have people from other parts of the world come to Canada and spend their money here. It would be a great help in remedying our balance of trade situation with the United States if the revenue we derive from the tourist business could be multiplied by ten times what it is today.
What I like most about this legislation are the mechanics of it. I am sure that if the opposition had been responsible for introducing such a measure we would have had another small loan bank similar to the industrial development bank, and God forbid that because in my opinion it would have simply resulted in the building up of another bureaucracy. I heard the speaker for the Liberal party refer to the industrial development bank and say that he was very strongly in favour of it. I took a look at the last financial statement of the bank and I find that although the bank has ten offices right across this country and over $1 million is involved in salaries the bank only made 537 loans. Just think what it is costing the country to maintain this bank and its employees. Compare that with any one of the chartered banks. They make thousands of loans. The total of their loans would be one hundred times as much as the loans made by the industrial development bank through its ten offices.
The Minister of Finance has, I am pleased to say, demonstrated to the business people of the country his interest in their affairs. During the recess I had the opportunity of discussing the situation with bankers, small businessmen and others and I should like to say that I do not think there has ever been


a minister of finance who has understood the problems of finance like the present Minister of Finance does.
It would have been very simple for the minister to set up a bank similar to the industrial development bank. However, as I have pointed out, this matter is to be handled through the well established channels of the chartered banks by authorizing them to make these loans for longer than the normal period of time. As a small businessman I remember quite well that in February, 1932, at the bottom of the depression, I went to a bank to borrow a few hundred dollars. I was entering into a partnership to carry on a business and I can remember the words of the manager of the bank very well. He said, "Go ahead and we will look after you". With that few hundred dollars and with a credit at the bank I was able to get along. How much simpler it would have been if I could have gone to the bank in 1932 and had my loan guaranteed as the small businessmen are now going to be able to do.
I think that the legislation will fill a great need in the business world in Canada today because we need an accumulation of small businesses across the country. After all, the companies that are large companies today were small companies 30, 40 or 50 years ago. What is being done by the government through this legislation is being done through the proper channels and will help to create a healthy climate. I congratulate the Minister of Finance on this measure and I am sure there will not be very much opposition to it.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after listening to the hon. member for York North I rise in a very humble mood as an ordinary backwoodsman to express my views on this measure. However, before proceeding with the few remarks I wish to make may I say that the hon. member mentioned that he did not understand what the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam had to say. The hon. member must suffer from defective hearing because the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam simply congratulated the minister on accepting a C.C.F. proposal which we have put forward for a number of years and also outlined the need and made a few suggestions with regard to the administration of the legislation.
The hon. member for York North also said that the Minister of Finance was the most wonderful minister of finance we have ever had because in introducing this measure he had not established what we might call a junior industrial development bank. Does the hon. member not realize that years ago governments set a pattern very similar to this with the business and professional loans act

under the veterans charter legislation and under the Farm Improvement Loans Act? The pattern has been set. We give the minister full credit for following a pattern that has been proved successful and following that example.
As a democratic socialist, Mr. Chairman, I support this measure which I consider to be a form of financial lifebelt being tossed out to rescue those in small business who only need one thing inasmuch as many of them have the ability and the assets, and that one thing is medium or long term credit. We support the legislation because we think it is very necessary indeed. You know, I am very inclined to localize. I am really a small-town person. I know numbers of merchants in my district who in the last year have discussed their needs in this direction with me; small industrialists, saw mill operators, tourist resort operators and so on who are not able to finance under the usual short term bank credit. It is because of the recognition of this need that we in this group, as always, are very pleased to see this resolution has been introduced.
Now, for instance, the district I represent does provide some of the greatest opportunities in Canada. The Kootenays provide the greatest opportunities to be found anywhere in Canada for the promotion and development of the tourist industry. There is no question about it. The Minister of Public Works has just written to me to say he is going to build another launchway for launches because of the development of the tourist industry. I am serious about this. The proposed measure will be of great assistance to a number of men who were born and raised in that country; who recognize the opportunities and who have properties. I am thinking of half a dozen men now who have the ability to work, and that is something very fortunate, and who have the will to work. All they need is money on long term credit. I know a number of men who will welcome this measure tonight. They are not necessarily members of the party to which I belong. I represent all the people in Kootenay West. I advocate anything that helps even the stray Conservative in there.
This is going to be a very fortunate piece of legislation. We will have to reserve our comments about the details until we see the bill. I feel that if this type of measure is administered soundly-I am not one who would suggest that two and two do not make four-then as soon as you pass this legislation you will have quite a number of people making application. As a matter of fact, most people think they are quite capable of operating some form of business. I have met some men who can talk for hours about how to
Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses run a business who could not operate a peanut stand when it comes to actually knowing what a man wants and administering a service. You will get large numbers who will apply who will not have the qualifications. They will find their outlets in other directions.
You are going to find large numbers of solid, good Canadians who know what they want and have the capacity to work, have the vision and have the ability to launch an industry and build it up slowly. This legislation will be of value to them. With sound administration and imagination this legislation could do a great deal toward removing this frightful situation which is developing in this country under a Conservative government, where we preach free enterprise and see legitimate free enterprise being destroyed all around us, that is what is happening today.
Yesterday I asked the Minister of National Revenue, a very kindly gentleman, a question concerning a matter which illustrates my point. There is a daily newspaper in my district which is very well established and possibly worth a million dollars. The newspaper owners own the local radio station. There is a little chap, a Canadian veteran, who comes along and establishes a newspaper which publishes every two weeks. His newspaper has a large circulation because he is a good photographer and he writes in a rather breezy way. He is getting support. He goes to the radio station and has flashes on the station, "buy the Kootenay Graphic at so and so's newsstand in Nelson or Trail". A few months ago this daily newspaper was publishing editorials urging people to vote for the free enterprise parties, support the spirit of competition. What do they do? The radio station writes to this little chap who is doing fairly well, who is just a little man trying to establish free enterprise, and tells him that because he is a competitor taking their advertising he will not be able to use their radio facilities again. This radio station operates under a licence issued by this government.
This is the sort of spirit that has to be overcome or we are going to build a monolithic state. If we have nothing in this country but large corporations and large unions, the ultimate result will be a monolithic state. We in this group believe that the safety of our society lies in the diversification of our economy, the diversification of political parties, the recognition of our different talents and so on, because in this way we get a variety of the blooms of civilization which come from genuine, legitimate competition.
I see the Minister of Finance looking rather uneasy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Would the hon. member permit a question?

Business of the House
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In his interesting peroration may I ask him to which party he was referring?

I am speaking here as a member of the C.C.F. party. I feel very keenly about this subject. I have noticed the deterioration, and with it not only comes deterioration in social ownership and personal ownership, but with this very development comes deterioration in character and, shall I say, stability. This is a commencement. I am speaking seriously. If this legislation turns out to be what we hope it is, and it is administered soundly and with imagination, it could do a great deal to restore to this country the economic democracy and the social democracy to which I am sure, regardless of party, we all subscribe.

May I call it ten o'clock?
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I ask the house leader if in announcing the business for tomorrow
he would indicate the order in which these resolutions will be taken.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We will continue with the resolution which has been under discussion pertaining to small businesses; following with the resolution standing in the name of the Minister of Public Works dealing with amendments to the National Housing Act; then the resolution in the name of the Minister of Labour dealing with the question of technical and vocational training; then the resolution in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce dealing with the establishment of a national productivity council.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I inquire if, when these resolutions are disposed of, we will be discussing the supplementary estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It depends on the speed with which the house progresses, Mr. Speaker. Our hope is that as these measures are presented here we will carry on with the second and third reading stages, so it is impossible to forecast the length of time consideration of the four measures will take.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, November 22, 1960
